newsitem.title: USA: "Old Ironsides" sailing ship tastes wind.
newsitem.headline: "Old Ironsides" sailing ship tastes wind.

text.p: The USS Constitution set its sails and briefly tasted the winds on Sunday while under tow from Boston Harbour about 20 miles north to Marblehead.
The Constitution, set to sail on its own for the first time in 116 years on Monday, unfurled its sails in slight winds while being towed by tugboats through Massachusetts Bay.

On Monday the tuboats will drop their lines and the frigate, nicknamed "Old Ironsides" during a victory over a British warship in the War of 1812, will sail on its own for about an hour. Weather forecasts are for slight winds and clear, sunny skies on Monday.
The officers of the Constitution were dressed in 1812 era uniforms on Sunday as they welcomed guests onboard the ship.
"It gives you a feeling of pride, a connection to the past," said Chief Petty Officer Joe Wilson. "She's all of America's ship and we can be proud of her."

Hundreds of spectators gathered at the Charlestown Navy Yard in Boston early Sunday to bid the ship off. Hundreds more greeted the Constitution and its crew as the ship was towed into the Marblehead harbour.
The Constitution was saluted by two modern American naval vessels during its short trip to Marblehead, which calls itself the birthplace of the U.S. Navy.
As Ironsides entered the Marblehead harbour, the ship shot a 21-gun salute to Fort Sewall, which responded with a single cannon blast.

The solo shot echoed an episode from the War of 1812, when the Constitution, pursued for three days by two larger British ships, took cover in the Marblehead harbour near the fort. The fort was armed by only a single cannonball and a handful of rocks. But its soldiers waited until the two British ships were within sight, shot the cannonball, and scared the British off.
